paragraphs.text: Lesson 12, meeting new people.
Lila and Beth are two college students who meet each other for the first time.
Listen to their conversation and try to answer the comprehension questions.
Oh, sorry. It looks like we're both reaching for the same book.
Oh, it's okay. The library is packed today, with exams coming up everyone's cramming like crazy.
Myself included. By the way, my name's Lila.
I'm Beth. I've seen you in Professor O'Malley's class. You sit in the back row. That's very smart.
I've seen you too. You've got guts sitting all the way in the front.
I kind of have to. Professor O'Malley's my uncle. And he always calls on me in class because he thinks I'm popular.
Are you? Are you kidding me? We're freshmen. The lowest on the totem pole around here.
Don't I know it. Last night, a junior cornered me and made me do her laundry.
All eight lobes, including her sweaty gym clothes.
Gross. Seems like the juniors and seniors treat freshmen like their personal slaves.
Last week a senior made me wash her car three times.
She said that learning to do the bidding of my superiors would prepare me for a future in the corporate world.
Seems like you and I have a lot in common. It's nice to meet someone else who is as miserable as I am.
Where are you from Lila? North Carolina. I'm from a town called Davell.
Hey, I'm from North Carolina too. Carrington. It's not too far from you. That's really a small world.
Yeah, you're the only person I've met from my neck of the woods. This college was tough to get into.
And because it's far from home, most of my friends chose to stay in town in a tense state.
Same with me. None of my friends back home wanted to move too far away.
I didn't either to be honest. But this is a good school. Besides, my uncle helped me get in.
My parents urged me to come here. And I was excited to start over with my social life.
I was a bit of a nerd back in high school. I got straight A's and well, I was a member of the marching band.
I was never one of the in crowd either. And I didn't even get asked to the prom.
Yep, joined the club. Neither did I. But who says we have to be known as nerds here?
And hey, next year we'll move up the food chain on campus. We could even make a pact.
A pact?
To stick together and help each other make it through the years ahead.
Hey, yeah. I love that idea.
Great. Well, I'll let you get back to studying. We can meet up later for dinner.
Let's learn the vocabulary from today's dialogue. Beth says the library is packed today.
The word pact means extremely crowded, full of people.
The reason the library is packed is that exams are coming up.
The phrasal verb coming up means happening soon.
And because exams are coming up, everyone's cramming like crazy.
The word cramming means studying very hard right before a test.
You're trying to put all the information into your head at the last minute. That's cramming.
Beth and Lila are in the same class. Lila sits in the back row, and Beth sits in the front.
Lila says, you've got guts sitting all the way in front.
You've got guts is a slang way to say you're brave, you're courageous.
Beth says she has to sit in front because the professor is one of her relatives.
She says, and he always calls on me in class because he thinks I'm popular.
Calls on me means selects me to answer a question in class.
Lila asks Beth if she is popular, and Beth responds, are you kidding me?
The verb kidding means joking, saying something that's not serious.
Beth and Lila are freshmen.
Freshmen are first-year university students.
And they're the lowest on the totem pole.
That's an expression meaning the lowest in the social hierarchy.
Among all the people in the school, they're considered the least important.
They have the lowest social status.
Lila says that last night a junior cornered her and made her do laundry.
A junior is a student in the third year of university.
Lila had to do eight loads of this person's laundry.
The word loads refers to baskets of dirty clothes.
Beth's reaction is gross.
The word gross means disgusting.
And Beth had a similar experience.
She had to wash the car of a senior student three times.
The senior student said that learning to do the bidding of one's superiors would help prepare for a future in the corporate world.
This expression, do someone's bidding, means submit to someone's orders, do what that person tells you to do.
So Lila and Beth are both miserable at their new college.
It turns out they're from the same state.
And Beth remarks, that's really a small world.
A small world is a surprising coincidence.
Lila says, you're the only person I've met from my neck of the woods.
My neck of the woods is an informal way to say my region or my neighborhood.
Most of Lila's friends chose to stay in town and attend state.
This means attend the local state university.
It was the same case with Beth.
Beth admits that she didn't want to move far away from home either, to be honest.
We usually use the phrase to be honest when expressing an opinion that may be unpopular or when revealing a secret thought or emotion, as in this case.
Lila says, my parents urged me to come to this university.
The verb urge means strongly encourage.
Lila says she was excited to start over with her social life.
She says, I was a bit of a nerd back in high school.
A nerd is a slang word for someone who is intelligent, but awkward.
They have few social skills. They're not considered cool or popular.
Lila said she got straight A's.
Straight A's means all high grades.
She performed very well academically.
Beth admits I was never one of the in-crowd either.
The in-crowd is the group of popular people.
And Lila shares another detail she didn't even get asked to the prom.
The prom is a big high school dance event that's considered a highlight of the year.
Beth says, yup, join the club, neither did I.
We use the expression join the club to say, I am or I was in the same bad situation.
It's like a way to say me too about being in bad situations.
Beth optimistically says that next year we'll move up the food chain on campus.
Move up the food chain means start increasing in the hierarchy, start increasing in social status.
And the word campus means the property of the college or university.
Beth suggests making a pact. What's a pact? That's a promise to each other.
Usually a very serious promise.
Beth suggests making a pact to stick together.
Stick together means stay together.
And help each other make it through the years ahead.
Make it in this context means successfully survive something difficult.
Indoor or keep going until finishing or achieving a goal.
Lila loves that idea and the two friends agree to meet up later for dinner.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
